1:
Every reader begins from the same scene. Delitzsch sets it out in full: the Pharisees are asked whose son the Christ is, answer David's, and are met with the question how David in the spirit calls him Lord — after which no man was able to answer a word. The inference, he notes, rests on two premises granted on both sides: that the psalm is David's and that it is prophetic of the Messiah. Augustine works the same question from the other end. We must not deny that Christ is David's son, or we contradict the opening of Matthew's Gospel; the Jews answered rightly, and the Gospel agrees with their answer. Calvin takes the Pharisees' silence as evidence: had any party among the Jews read the psalm differently, they would certainly have used that difference to escape the difficulty. Henry adds the argument from dignity — as the greatness of Melchizedek is proved by Abraham paying him tithes, so the dignity of Christ is proved by David, that great man, calling him his Lord.

Who else the psalm might describe is canvassed at length and dismissed. Clarke reports the attempts: some give it to Eliezer, Abraham's steward, on the victory over the four kings; others to David after the Philistines; others to Solomon, Hezekiah or Zerubbabel. The bare reading of the psalm shows the vanity of these, since the king described is David's Lord, sits at God's right hand, reigns from eternity, has an everlasting priesthood and judges all nations; there never was such a prince, nor can be. Ellicott lists six proposals — the Messiah, David himself, Solomon, Hezekiah, Joshua son of Josedech, and one of the Asmonean priest-kings — and notes the second is inconsistent with the psalm being David's. Calvin's argument is narrower and harder. Grant that the kingdom of Christ is typified in David; still it cannot be said of David or any successor that he was to be a priest not according to the law but after the order of Melchizedek, and that for ever, since no new priestly dignity could then be instituted without robbing the house of Levi, and perpetuity in that office belongs to no man whose life is short and uncertain. Clarke also records a middle course. Venema read it as a divine oracle partly of David's Lord and partly of David himself, dated a little after the ark was brought home, when the kingdom was confirmed but not yet extended.

The seat at the right hand is where the readings part. Ellicott will not have much pressed from it. Commentators have hunted through Arabian custom and even Greek mythology for proof that the phrase means viceroyalty or copartnership in the throne, but the nearest thing in the Old Testament makes it only a mark of extreme honour, as with Bathsheba; and the psalm itself later puts the Lord at the right hand of the person addressed, so the position should not be pressed in either case. Henry presses it hard instead, hearing three things in the posture: sitting is a resting posture, after his labours; a ruling posture, to give law and judgment; and a remaining posture, for he sits like a king for ever. Wesley reads the decree as made from eternity and executed at the resurrection, and takes the footstool for slaves and vassals. Spurgeon dwells on the speech itself — how condescending that a mortal ear should hear and a human pen record this secret converse — and notes that David, firm believer in the divine unity as he was, distinguishes the two persons and claims a peculiar interest in the second by calling him mine.

Clarke closes with the manuscripts. One appears to read Jehovah said unto Jehovah in place of unto my Lord; eight drop the prefix on footstool and read it as a genitive with the Greek and Latin, and many make it singular.
2:
The rod is taken by nearly everyone as a sceptre and by nearly everyone as the gospel. Gill makes it the sceptre of righteousness, first preached in Zion and carried thence into all the world; he adds that the Jews own it for a rod in the Messiah's hand but understand it literally, having a fabulous notion that it was the rod held by Jacob, Judah, Moses, Aaron, David and every king of Judah down to the destruction of the temple. Clarke says the same, adding that the gospel extends a moralizing influence over multitudes who do not receive it to their salvation. Wesley reasons from the nature of the kingdom — since it is not carnal but spiritual, the sceptre is nothing else but his word. Ellicott works on the grammar. The verb should be rendered stretch, as of stretching out the hand; the word differs from the rod of an earlier psalm and is no weapon of destruction but the emblem of kingly rule; and the command to rule is better taken as spoken by the Lord, who seats the earthly monarch beside him, takes his sceptre and stretches it over the surrounding nations. In the midst, rather than over, states the condition under which the sovereignty is assumed.

The day of power is read as a muster. Delitzsch gives it as the day when the king calls up his levy for battle, and renders the people's response as willingnesses, entire cheerful readiness: no lengthy proclamation is needed, for this is no army of mercenaries but men who present themselves from inward impulse. Ellicott translates it thy people will be willing on thy muster-day, and reports a variant of one letter giving on the holy mountains, supported by many manuscripts, which yields a picture of the people gathering on the hills round Zion. Gill runs the day of power through three senses: the first age of the gospel, when the oracles ceased; the whole gospel dispensation; or, as he prefers, the set time of love and life at each conversion.

On the willing people Clarke turns and fights. The verse, he says, has been woefully perverted into a proof of irresistible grace; whether that doctrine be true or false, it is not in this text. Much has been spoken against free will by men who seem not to have understood the term: the phrase is as absurd as bound will, since it is not will if it is not free. If a man is forced to believe, it is the forcing power that believes, not the machine forced; if he cannot will good and refuse evil he cannot be saved as a rational being, and if he acts only under compulsion he cannot be damned. He then puts the Hebrew against the reading, translating thy princely or free people in the day of thy power, and marshals the versions: the Chaldee makes it a people who willingly labour in the law; the Latin and Greek read the first word as a principle or beginning, referred by their interpreters to the divinity of Christ and illustrated from the opening of John; the Arabic makes it the government existing with him.

The last clause defeats them all in different ways. Ellicott renders it from the womb of morning dew of thy youth, and says the words alone would describe the vigour and freshness of the person addressed, but the parallelism points back to the gathering army; dew was a familiar emblem of multitude and freshness, and here of brightness, so that the young warriors come thick and bright as morning dew; he quotes Milton on the innumerable angel host. Wesley reads the same figure as offspring, the church more numerous than the drops, and takes the beauties of holiness for robes of righteousness; the people, he adds, offer themselves as living sacrifices and freewill offerings rather than oxen or sheep.
4:
Why God should swear at all is the first question. Gill answers from the doubts the oath was meant to settle: whether the Aaronic priesthood was really changed, seeing it had been given to Phinehas for an everlasting priesthood; whether so great a person as the Son of God could be called a priest; and how he could be one at all, being of Judah, of which nothing was said of priesthood. It was less for Christ's sake than his people's. Clarke makes it an irresistible decree, without condition or contingency, with nothing left to the will of man or angel. Wesley reduces it to a clause: that the priesthood might be sure and irrevocable. Spurgeon dwells on the double assurance: it must be a solemn matter that leads the Eternal to swear, and as if to make it sure it is added that he will not repent; the declaration runs in the present tense, thou art, as being the only time with the Lord.

What kind of priest is meant turns on two words. Clarke observes that the Hebrew means not only priest but prince, since in patriarchal times heads of families exercised both political and sacerdotal authority; he gives the priest a threefold office — instructor, sacrificer, mediator — and finds all three in Christ. He also reports Calmet's three orders of priesthood — royalty, treated by nearly every nation as the natural right of kings, the first-born, and the Levites — of which the last two ended with the Jewish polity. On Melchizedek he notes that Salem is Jerusalem, and that the elements of the name mean peace and righteousness, which is why Christ is styled the Prince of peace and king in the empire of righteousness. Ellicott corrects the rendering: better after the manner of than after the order, since the psalmist could have had no intention of contrasting this priesthood with Aaron's, natural only once that order was visibly doomed. The previous history offered no example of the formal union of the two offices; it appears first as an idea in Zechariah and in fact under Jonathan; though the two functions were sometimes joined, notably where David's sons are called priests, it was necessary to go back to Melchizedek, in whom history recognised the union.

The fifth verse reverses the posture, and nobody is quite easy about it. Gill offers three constructions — the words directed to Christ, at whose right hand the Lord helps him; to the church, at whose right hand he stands ready to save; or rather to the Father, at whose right hand David's Lord sits. Henry canvasses the same three, prefers the last, and remarks that Christ's sitting at God's right hand speaks as much terror to his enemies as comfort to his people. Ellicott settles it by the vocabulary: the word here is used nowhere else but of God, and since God has throughout been the active agent while the king was addressed, the king must still be addressed, and the shift of the divine position from his right hand to his left is only the usage of the language — to sit at the right hand was an emblem of honour, to stand there a figure of protecting might, and the battle now beginning called for the second. Delitzsch reaches the same result from the accents: the victorious work of the person addressed is not his own but the Lord's through him.

Clarke, following Venema, thinks the psalm turns here to David, and hears in the striking through of kings an allusion to Abraham's defeat of the four kings — the more likely because Melchizedek meets Abraham in that chapter. Spurgeon reads it of the end instead: the Priest-King will not for ever sit waiting but will lead the final charge in person, and a single stroke will suffice, as when the angel smote Herod.
6:
Judging among the heathen is taken three ways. Gill allows either rule — making the Gentiles obedient, reigning in their hearts, enlarging the dominion from sea to sea — or the infliction of judgments, and names the objects of the second: the Papists, the nations that will be angry when the time of wrath is come, whom Christ will break with his iron rod. Clarke reads it first of David extending his dominion over the Idumeans, Moabites and Philistines, filling pits with slain until the neighbouring kings pay him tribute. Wesley states the warning the others leave implicit: such passages are not to be understood grossly but spiritually, according to the nature of Christ's kingdom. Ellicott works on the Hebrew, where heathen and corpses play on each other. A slight change of pointing gives a better construction than the Authorised Version's: he judges among the heathen fulness of corpses; the poet, he suggests, first meant fulness of judgment and altered it for the sound. The wounded head he takes as a crushed host over a vast land, the word meaning a band of men, though others understand the chief of a wide country.

Clarke identifies that head. It must be someone of very extensive sway, and he proposes Antichrist, with so many countries under his spiritual domination; the priesthood not after the order of Melchizedek shall be destroyed, and every government not modelled on the eternal King and Priest with it. Asked who this usurping power is, he points at an Italian archbishop.

The brook divides them more evenly. Gill reports the reading that makes it Christ's sufferings, with a possible allusion to the black brook over which David passed in his distress and Christ went into the garden where his sorrows began; but since the clause is surrounded by others speaking only of victory and triumph, he judges those nearer the truth who make it Christ's conquest over sin, Satan, the world and death, comparing the prophecy that he shall drink of the blood of the slain, or who hear the eagerness of a general pursuing a routed army. Ellicott takes that last picture without hesitation: the victorious leader, faint yet pursuing, pauses at the stream crossing his path and then, refreshed and with head erect, continues after the foe. He meets the objection that a thirsty warrior is unworthy of the divine subject — poetry knows nothing of such timidity, and beside the blood-stained hero of Isaiah this detail is mild. Clarke and Wesley keep the harder reading. Wesley makes the waters afflictions, borne before the honour of sitting at the right hand; Clarke says he shall suffer sorely and even die in the struggle, and that lifting up the head is the rising from the dead and the ascent to glory.

Clarke ends with a key he offers as his own. The psalm, he says, is a war song, and every phrase in it is military: the proclamation of the divine purpose; the battle and victory foretold in the footstool; the ensign displayed, the rod being the pole on which the banner is raised; the motto inscribed on it, rule thou in the midst of thine enemies; the muster of volunteers, neither kidnapped nor impressed, every man bringing gifts to his General and King; the regimentals, the beauties of holiness being splendid garments showing the richness of the King and the worth of the soldiers, as the Lacedaemonians went into battle in scarlet and never without crowns and garlands; the troops innumerable as the drops of dew at break of day; the commission of the priest-commander after the plan of that ancient king; the victory gained while the Conqueror sits at the right hand on high; judgment executed; false religion brought down; refreshment at a rivulet met providentially in the way; and at last the emperor proclaimed, his soldiers seated with him on the same throne.
